interviewQuestions.question: Can you override a static method in Java?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
No — you can hide a static method with the same signature in a subclass, but you can't override it. Overriding relies on the object's actual runtime type, resolved through a vtable at the moment of the call. Static methods belong to the class itself, not to any instance, so there's no object to look a runtime type up on — the compiler resolves the call using the reference's declared type, at compile time.

I'd show it concretely: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.identify();` prints `Animal`, not `Dog`, because `a` is declared as `Animal` — even though the object underneath is a `Dog`. If `identify()` were an instance method with `@Override`, it would correctly print `Dog`.

I'd close by naming this as Java/C#-specific — it comes from having a real compile-time type system that dynamic languages like Python don't enforce the same way.

**Testing:** whether you know the mechanism (compile-time reference-type binding) behind the one-word answer, not just the word itself.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The core trap question

interviewQuestions.question: What actually happens if you try to override a static method — does the code even compile?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It compiles and runs fine — nothing throws, no error, no warning by default. What happens instead is method hiding: the subclass's static method with the matching signature quietly shadows the parent's, but only for calls made through the subclass's own type or a subclass instance. Any call routed through a supertype-typed reference still resolves to the supertype's version.

That's the trap — a candidate who assumes "if it compiles and runs, it must be doing what I expect" will confidently predict the subclass's output and be wrong. I'd walk through the exact case: `Animal a = new Dog();` then `a.identify()` prints `Animal`, because the call is bound to the declared type before the program ever runs, not decided fresh based on what `a` happens to point to.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish "compiles without error" from "behaves the way I'd naively guess."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What happens when you try it

interviewQuestions.question: Does this static-vs-instance dispatch distinction apply the same way in other languages, like Python or JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Not in the same rigid way. Java and C# enforce a hard compile-time line between static and instance dispatch because they have a real static type system to bind calls against. Python and JavaScript resolve most calls dynamically at runtime through attribute or prototype lookup, so a Python `@staticmethod` can be shadowed on a subclass, but the mechanism looks more like ordinary attribute resolution than Java's declared-reference-type binding — there's no separate "compile-time dispatch" step happening.

I'd frame the general lesson rather than overclaiming: languages with a real static type system tend to bind static calls early and rigidly; dynamically-typed languages resolve nearly everything late, so the specific "hiding, not overriding" trap is much less sharp outside Java-like languages.

**Testing:** whether you can generalize the underlying principle (early binding vs late binding) without incorrectly asserting the exact Java rule holds everywhere.
